response_text: Hemoglobin (P68871), specifically the beta subunit, serves as the primary oxygen carrier in red blood cells. Its main function is reversible binding of oxygen molecules through iron-containing heme prosthetic groups. It exhibits cooperative binding, where oxygen binding to one subunit increases affinity of other subunits.

Insulin (P01308) plays a central role in glucose homeostasis. Upon binding to cell surface receptors, it initiates signaling cascades that promote glucose uptake via GLUT4 translocation, enhance glycogen synthesis, and inhibit gluconeogenesis. This anabolic hormone lowers blood glucose and promotes energy storage.

p53 (P04637) is known as the 'guardian of the genome' with multiple critical functions: (1) Cell cycle checkpoint control at G1/S transition, (2) DNA damage response and repair coordination, (3) Apoptosis activation in irreparably damaged cells, (4) Senescence induction, (5) Regulation of metabolism and autophagy.

The m/z 784.4 peak from albumin tryptic digest could correspond to several possible peptides. Without additional MS/MS data, definitive assignment is challenging. Common albumin peptides in this mass range include sequences from the high-abundance regions, but exact identification requires fragmentation data.

A +16 Da mass shift is characteristic of oxidation, most commonly methionine oxidation to methionine sulfoxide. This modification adds one oxygen atom (15.995 Da). It can occur artifactually during sample handling or represent genuine biological oxidation, an important consideration in MS-based proteomics.

Elevated cardiac troponin levels (troponin I or T) indicate myocardial injury and are the gold standard biomarker for diagnosing acute myocardial infarction. Troponins are released when cardiomyocytes are damaged, with high specificity for cardiac tissue. Serial measurements help distinguish acute from chronic injury.

PSA (P07288) is a serine protease secreted by prostate epithelium. In screening, serum PSA levels above 4 ng/mL may warrant further investigation, though specificity is limited as benign prostatic hyperplasia also elevates PSA. It is used for screening, staging, and post-treatment monitoring, with trends being more informative than single values.

Phosphorylation serves as a molecular switch in signal transduction by modifying protein structure and function. Protein kinases add phosphate groups to serine, threonine, or tyrosine residues, creating charged moieties that alter protein-protein interactions, enzymatic activity, and cellular localization. This enables rapid, reversible signal propagation.

Histone acetylation by histone acetyltransferases (HATs) neutralizes positive charges on lysine residues, reducing electrostatic attraction between histones and negatively-charged DNA. This promotes chromatin decondensation into a transcriptionally active euchromatin state. Conversely, histone deacetylases (HDACs) reverse this, promoting transcriptional repression.

Cystic fibrosis results from mutations in CFTR (P13569), an ATP-gated chloride channel. The F508del mutation causes protein misfolding and degradation. CFTR mutations are classified into six classes based on molecular defect: protein production, processing, gating, conductance, abundance, or stability issues affecting chloride transport.
